title: Female Flower, Bract, Stigma, and Inflorescence Anatomy
objective: Identify female reproductive structures without using the colloquial word “calyx” for every surrounding tissue.

terms.definition: A modified leaf associated with a flower or inflorescence.
The receptive surface on which pollen can hydrate and germinate.
The structure containing the ovule and later contributing to fruit formation.

coreScience: Female cannabis inflorescences are made of many small pistillate flowers associated with bracts and small leaves. Each pistillate flower contains a one-ovule ovary and two elongated stigmatic branches that extend outward. The surrounding bract becomes a prominent resin-bearing tissue and is one of the densest sites of capitate-stalked glandular trichomes.

Cannabis literature and grower language use “bract” and “calyx” inconsistently. This encyclopedia adopts the following controlled convention: calyx means the collective sepal whorl, while the prominent resin-bearing leaf-like structure surrounding the pistillate flower is labeled the bract. That is a declared terminology choice tied to the cited anatomical sources, not a claim that every publication uses the terms identically.

The commercial “bud” is an inflorescence, not a single flower. Its density, branching, bract size, leaf proportion, stigma development, trichome distribution, and maturation pattern vary with genetics and environment. Pollination changes resource allocation toward achene and embryo development.

The apparent bulk of a mature female inflorescence reflects repeated floral units, subtending bracts, reduced leaves, branch architecture, and tissue expansion rather than enlargement of one flower. Trichome density and morphology differ among organs, and pollination changes developmental priorities as ovules and embryos mature. Because floral tissues age at different rates within the canopy, stigma color, bract swelling, and trichome appearance should be sampled from defined positions instead of treated as a single whole-plant maturity signal.
cultivationRelevance: Sample maturity from defined bract locations rather than whichever visible leaf has the most dramatic trichome color. Sugar-leaf glands and bract glands can mature differently.
When inspecting for disease, open dense inflorescences carefully. Exterior appearance can hide senescent tissue, moisture pockets, insects, or Botrytis injury.

Use a defined floral sampling plan for maturity, pathology, or chemistry work. Record branch, canopy level, tissue type, bract versus sugar leaf, and developmental stage before imaging or collecting laboratory material. This prevents top-canopy or leaf-biased samples from being generalized to the entire crop.

Dense inflorescences require internal as well as external inspection. When disease risk is suspected, gently separate tissue at representative sites and record moisture exposure, necrosis, odor, insects, lesions, and progression. Exterior trichome abundance or stigma color should never be used to rule out hidden tissue damage.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Record plant ID, branch, canopy level, main or lateral position, and developmental stage. Use the same positional rule across repeated sampling so maturation differences are not created by changing the sample site.

Record emerging stigmas, active flowering, stigma senescence, bract expansion, pollination evidence, seed development, or tissue senescence. Keep stigma color separate from other maturity observations.
Record exact tissue type, bract or leaf, surface orientation, magnification, image scale, lighting, and representative sample count. Compare like tissue with like tissue across dates.

Record whether inflorescence tissue is compact or open, trapped moisture, necrosis, lesions, pest signs, fungal growth, odor, or tissue collapse. Photograph both exterior and opened interior when documenting a disorder.

Record swollen ovaries/achenes, known pollen exposure, pollination date if controlled, and distribution of seed set. Pollination can alter morphology and chemistry and should be separated from unpollinated maturity.
If chemistry, pathogen, or moisture testing is performed, record sample ID, tissue/position, collection time, laboratory, method, and link the result back to the exact floral observation.

misconceptions: A bud is one flower: It is a compound inflorescence containing many small flowers and bracts.
Every swollen resinous structure is a calyx: The commonly referenced structure is usually the bract.
Orange stigmas alone establish harvest maturity: Stigma color is affected by age, pollination, handling, and environment and is only one observation.
evidenceLimits: Cannabis floral terminology is inconsistent across botanical and cultivation literature, particularly around 'bract' and 'calyx,' so this encyclopedia uses an explicit declared convention. Visible stigma color, trichome appearance, or bract swelling are descriptive maturity indicators rather than validated standalone assays for cannabinoid concentration, terpene profile, disease absence, or optimal harvest date. Sampling position, genotype, pollination status, and environment can all alter the observed pattern.
